lines.L02: Without a calibration, nobody can say.
lines.L03: In the analyzer, light passes through the reaction cuvette; the photometer measures absorbance.
lines.L04: The concentration is then calculated from a calibration.
lines.L05: More light absorbed means less reaches the detector — and a higher absorbance.
lines.L06: Calibrators have assigned values; each level gives one signal.
lines.L07: Plot absorbance against concentration, point by point.
lines.L08: A least-squares line through the points is the calibration curve.
lines.L09: Slope, intercept and R² are computed from these points.
lines.L10: A control with a known target is read off the curve.
lines.L11: R² alone is not enough: residuals should be small, with no trend.
lines.L12: Acceptance limits come from your IFU and SOP.
lines.L13: LabGuide doesn’t calibrate the analyzer — it records how calibration was done.
lines.L14: Instrument, analyte, reagent REF, IFU revision — and no guessed parameters.
lines.L15: Then the record: calibrator lot, assigned values, unit — from the value sheet.
lines.L16: “Accepted” is blocked until QC after calibration has passed…
lines.L17: …and until an authorized person is named.
lines.L18: Saved records go to the calibration log — on this device.
lines.L19: Create, edit, delete — each leaves a history entry, even after deletion.
lines.L20: Calibration is not just a curve. It’s confidence in every result.
